parsed.title: Discussion on taxes, domain, and low‑profit app ideas

claims.text: Author paid 500 UAH to aunt Sveta to correct a large tax‑declaration mistake and avoided larger fines by re‑filing correctly (about 1000 UAH paid).
The inspector had not reviewed the author’s declarations for 1.5 years, simply approved them, then was reprimanded and began demanding re‑checks of all years.
The main difficulty is not calculating tax amounts but ensuring each column is correctly matched and subtractions are applied.
The whole procedure can be done in about an hour with Excel, roughly one day per month.
Participant P2 states they have not bought a domain.
P4 jokes that nobody would buy a domain.
P1 sarcastically suggests that buying a calculator would free up money for a domain.

topics.title: Profit potential of a lightweight web/app product

claims.text: Web is the simplest platform but less profitable than Android/iOS; SEO is poor, no external traffic, and app stores promote new apps more effectively.
User retention is near zero because a paywall appears within the first 10 seconds, deterring purchases.
Conversion is assumed to be negligible; the product lacks bank or tax‑payer‑cabinet integrations.
A successful case mentioned requires fast delivery (< 1 week) and a cross‑platform stack (Flutter), copying popular features with minor tweaks.
P1 doubts anyone would buy this product after a few months.
The calculator only works with hryvnia‑based FOP; the author had to convert all transactions using the daily exchange rate.

topics.title: Security concerns and price expectations for the app

claims.text: P4 suggests the app is marketed as a local‑first tool with USD/UAH rates updated every 5 minutes, but the paid bundle actually contains the source code.
P4 implies the password is stored in local storage as a 100 % discount promo code.
P1 believes most LinkedIn users could hack the app easily.
P5 labels the approach as piracy and jokes about asking the developer for the password.
